title: Himachali Siddu: How To Make the Mountain Bread That Fueled Himalayan Shepherds
excerpt: This steamed, walnut-stuffed bread from Himachal Pradesh is centuries old, protein-rich, and easy to make at home with just wheat flour, yeast, and a handful of nuts and herbs.
body:
• Siddu is a traditional fermented and steamed bread from Himachal Pradesh, stuffed with a coarsely ground walnut-and-herb paste
  • Historically carried by nomadic shepherds as portable sustenance during long mountain treks, the dish dates back at least 200 years
  • The name may derive from the Tibetan word "tse-doe" (steamed bread), reflecting cross-Himalayan cultural exchange along ancient trade routes
  • Unlike fried snacks, siddu is steamed, making it a lighter, gut-friendly option for the monsoon season

When the monsoon rains sweep across Himachal Pradesh, locals turn to a food that has sustained mountain communities for centuries: siddu. This steamed, stuffed bread — part dumpling, part bao, entirely Himachali — is one of India's most underappreciated regional dishes, and one of the easiest to make at home.

Siddu is made from fermented whole wheat dough filled with a coarse paste of walnuts, onions, garlic, ginger, green chillies, and fresh herbs. The filled dough is shaped into half-moons, steamed for 25 to 30 minutes, and served dripping with ghee alongside green or red chutney and dal.

A Shepherd's Food, Centuries Old

The dish is believed to have originated in the Mahasu region, part of present-day Shimla district, before spreading across Himachal Pradesh. For generations, nomadic shepherds in the state carried siddu on long, gruelling treks through the mountains — its combination of fermented carbohydrates and protein-rich walnut filling made it the ideal portable meal.

"This is an invaluable traditional food in Himachali culture. For 200 years we have been making and customizing the recipe."

— Shakuntala, siddu maker at Kulture Café, Old Manali

The name itself may carry traces of cross-border exchange. Some food historians link "siddu" to the Tibetan word "tse-doe," meaning steamed bread, a nod to the culinary traffic that once moved along Himalayan trade routes connecting present-day Himachal Pradesh with Tibet and China.

Versatile and Adaptable

No two siddus are exactly alike. The classic filling uses soaked walnuts as the base, but across the state, variations abound: poppy seeds, almonds, apricots, and sesame seeds are common additions. In some households, paneer, green peas, or even minced mutton replace the nut filling. A sweet version — stuffed with desiccated coconut, jaggery, and sesame — is also popular.

The dish has drawn comparisons to steamed and stuffed breads from across the world: Tibetan shapale, Russian chebureki, Chinese bao, and South American empanadas. What distinguishes siddu is the fermentation step — the yeast-risen dough gives it a soft, spongy texture that absorbs ghee and chutney beautifully.

The Recipe

For the dough: Combine 2 cups whole wheat flour, salt to taste, and 1 tablespoon active dry yeast in a large bowl. Add warm water gradually and knead into a soft, pliable dough. Cover and let rise in a warm place for 1 to 2 hours until doubled.

For the stuffing: In a mixer or blender, coarsely grind 1/2 cup walnuts with 1 chopped onion, 7-8 garlic cloves, 1 inch of ginger, 4-5 green chillies, a handful each of fresh coriander and mint leaves, 1 teaspoon cumin seeds, 1 teaspoon whole coriander seeds, 1 teaspoon black peppercorns, salt, and a splash of water. The mixture should be coarse, not a smooth paste.

To assemble: Divide the risen dough into 4 equal portions. Roll or flatten each piece into a disc, place a generous spoonful of stuffing in the center, and fold into a half-moon shape. Pinch the edges tightly to seal.

To cook: Place the filled siddus in a greased steamer and steam for 25 to 30 minutes. The bread should be cooked through — test with a toothpick. Serve immediately, drizzled generously with desi ghee, alongside green chutney or dal.

Why Siddu Matters for the Diaspora

For Indian families abroad missing the flavors of pahadi cuisine, siddu is remarkably accessible. Every ingredient — wheat flour, yeast, walnuts, basic spices — is available at any grocery store. It requires no special equipment beyond a steamer (a colander set over a pot of boiling water works fine), and the entire process from dough to plate takes about two hours, most of it hands-off rising time.

As monsoon comfort foods go, siddu offers something fried snacks cannot: the slow satisfaction of fermented bread, the crunch of walnut, and a direct line to a mountain food tradition that has fed shepherds and families alike for centuries.
